cards.front: What is biodegradable waste? Give four examples.
cards.back: Biodegradable waste is waste that can be broken down by microorganisms (bacteria, fungi) into simpler natural substances over a period of time. It was once living matter or derived from living things. Examples: vegetable and fruit peels, leftover cooked food, leaves and garden waste, paper and cardboard, cotton cloth, wood shavings. Biodegradable waste decomposes in days to months and ultimately becomes soil nutrients.
cards.memory_hook: Bio = life. Biodegradable = broken down BY life. If it was once alive (plant leaf, food, paper from trees) → it can be broken down by other life (bacteria). Banana peel + time + microbes = soil. Simple as that.

cards.front: What is non-biodegradable waste? Give four examples.
cards.back: Non-biodegradable waste is waste that cannot be broken down by microorganisms naturally, or takes hundreds to thousands of years to do so. It accumulates in the environment. Examples: plastic bags and bottles (100–1000 years to degrade), glass (millions of years), aluminium cans (80–200 years), synthetic rubber (50–80 years), electronic waste, batteries. Non-biodegradable waste is the main cause of long-term environmental pollution.
cards.memory_hook: Non-biodegradable = nature can't eat it. Microbes look at plastic and say 'not my food.' A plastic bag thrown today will outlive you, your children, and your grandchildren. That's the terrifying truth about non-biodegradable waste.

cards.front: Classify these items as biodegradable or non-biodegradable: paper, plastic bottle, vegetable peels, glass jar, cotton shirt, aluminium foil.
cards.back: Biodegradable: Paper (made from wood/plant fibres — decomposes in weeks), vegetable peels (organic — decomposes in days), cotton shirt (natural plant fibre — decomposes in months to years). Non-biodegradable: Plastic bottle (petroleum-derived — takes 450+ years), glass jar (mineral-based — millions of years), aluminium foil (metal — 80–200 years). Key note: paper and cotton are often confused with non-biodegradable because they look processed, but they are plant-derived and DO biodegrade.
cards.memory_hook: Rule of thumb: Came from plants/animals = biodegradable. Made in a factory from chemicals/minerals = non-biodegradable. Paper = from trees = plant = biodegradable. Plastic = from petroleum = factory = NOT biodegradable.

cards.front: What is a landfill? Why is it a problem?
cards.back: A landfill is a large area where municipal solid waste (garbage) is deposited, compacted, and buried underground. Problems: (1) Limited capacity — landfills fill up quickly in urban areas. (2) Leachate — toxic liquid formed when rainwater dissolves chemicals from garbage; it contaminates groundwater and nearby soil. (3) Methane gas — anaerobic decomposition of organic waste produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. (4) Land is wasted for decades. (5) Attracts rodents, flies; spreads disease. (6) Foul odour. Landfills are not a sustainable solution to waste management.
cards.memory_hook: Landfill = land filled with problems. Five evils: CLMD+D = Capacity limit, Leachate, Methane, Disease, Dirty land forever. The world's first cities created the world's first landfills — and we're still paying for that mistake.

cards.front: What is leachate? Why is it dangerous?
cards.back: Leachate is the toxic liquid produced when rainwater seeps through a landfill, dissolving and picking up harmful chemicals, heavy metals, and organic compounds from the garbage. It then seeps into the soil and groundwater below the landfill. Danger: Leachate contains heavy metals (lead, mercury, cadmium), toxic organic compounds, and pathogens. When it contaminates groundwater, it pollutes drinking water sources (wells, bore wells) for communities living near the landfill. It is one of the most serious environmental hazards of landfills.
cards.memory_hook: Leachate = garbage tea. Just as water seeping through tea leaves becomes tea, rainwater seeping through garbage becomes toxic 'garbage tea' — and it drips into the groundwater where people get their drinking water. Disgusting and dangerous.

cards.front: What is composting? How does it work?
cards.back: Composting is the process of converting biodegradable organic waste (vegetable peels, fruit scraps, leaves, garden waste) into compost — a rich, dark, crumbly manure — through the action of microorganisms (bacteria, fungi). Process: organic waste is collected in a pit or bin, kept moist and aerated, and microorganisms decompose it over 4–8 weeks. The resulting compost improves soil fertility, water retention, and structure. Composting returns nutrients to the soil and diverts biodegradable waste from landfills. Add: green waste (food scraps) + brown waste (dry leaves, paper). Do NOT add: meat, oily food, dairy (these attract pests).
cards.memory_hook: Composting = kitchen waste gets a second life as garden superfood. Peels in, compost out. Microbes do the work for free. Every compost pit is a little factory turning garbage into garden gold.

cards.front: What is vermicomposting? How is it different from regular composting?
cards.back: Vermicomposting is a type of composting that uses earthworms to break down organic waste. Earthworms eat organic matter and their castings (excretions, also called worm poop or vermicompost) are extremely rich in nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and beneficial microorganisms — far more nutritious than regular compost. Differences from regular composting: faster process (2–4 weeks vs. 4–8 weeks), richer product, can be done indoors in a small bin, produces no bad odour when done correctly, and the worms themselves are a valuable by-product (sold for fishing bait, bird feed, or to start new vermicompost units).
cards.memory_hook: Vermi = worm (from Latin 'vermis'). Vermicompost = worm compost = worm poop. Earthworms are the original recyclers — they've been turning dead matter into rich soil for 600 million years. Give them your kitchen scraps; they'll give you gold for your garden.

cards.front: What are the 3Rs of waste management? List them in order of importance.
cards.back: The 3Rs are: (1) Reduce — most important; generate less waste in the first place by consuming less, avoiding unnecessary packaging, choosing reusable over single-use. (2) Reuse — use items again instead of discarding; reuse bags, containers, paper, glass bottles. (3) Recycle — least preferable of the three, but far better than landfilling; convert waste into new materials. The order matters: Reducing waste is always better than managing it after it is generated. Recycling still uses energy and water, so it is the last resort before landfilling.
cards.memory_hook: 3Rs ladder from best to least: Reduce (rung 1 — TOP), Reuse (rung 2), Recycle (rung 3 — bottom). Going down means more environmental impact. Always climb as high as possible. 'Reduce' is royalty; 'Recycle' is the last resort.

cards.front: Why is 'Reduce' the most important of the 3Rs?
cards.back: Reduce is the most important because it prevents waste from being generated in the first place — there is nothing to manage, collect, transport, process, or dispose of. Every other R (Reuse, Recycle) still requires energy, water, and resources to process. Reducing also conserves raw materials (trees for paper, petroleum for plastic) and avoids all the environmental impacts of production. For example, not buying a plastic-wrapped snack avoids: the plastic production, the packaging waste, the transport emissions, and the disposal. One reduction = many avoided harms.
cards.memory_hook: The best garbage is garbage that was never created. Reduce = zero waste problem. Compare: Reduce = not starting a fire. Reuse = putting the fire out once. Recycle = using the ashes. Obviously, not starting it is best.

cards.front: Give two examples each of Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle in daily school life.
cards.back: Reduce: (1) Print on both sides of paper — use 50% less paper. (2) Bring food in a tiffin box instead of buying packaged snacks — reduces packaging waste. Reuse: (1) Use both sides of notebook pages before discarding. (2) Use old newspaper as book covers instead of plastic sheet. (3) Reuse old bags for carrying items. Recycle: (1) Collect all used paper, cardboard, and plastic bottles and give them to a kabadiwala (scrap dealer). (2) Donate old books to juniors rather than discarding them — this is reuse, but giving waste paper to recyclers is recycling.
cards.memory_hook: School 3R actions — R1: Print double-sided (Reduce). R2: Use both sides of notebook (Reuse). R3: Give paper to kabadiwala (Recycle). Three actions, same school day, three different levels of waste management.

cards.front: Why is burning garbage harmful? What does it release?
cards.back: Burning garbage is highly harmful because it releases toxic air pollutants: (1) Dioxins and furans — among the most toxic chemicals known; carcinogenic (cancer-causing). (2) Carbon monoxide (CO) — poisonous gas that reduces oxygen-carrying capacity of blood. (3) Particulate matter (PM2.5) — tiny particles that enter deep into lungs. (4) Carbon dioxide — greenhouse gas. (5) Toxic fumes from burning plastic: hydrogen chloride, styrene. Effects: respiratory diseases (asthma, bronchitis), cancer risk, global warming. Burning garbage in open areas or at landfills is illegal under India's Solid Waste Management Rules 2016, yet it remains common in many areas.
cards.memory_hook: Burning garbage = releasing everything bad at once. Landfill buries the problem; burning makes everyone breathe it. DCPC = Dioxins, CO, Particulates, CO₂ — the toxic cocktail of burning garbage. The smoke from burning one plastic bag contains more dioxins than a cigarette.

cards.front: What is source segregation? Why is it the first step in effective waste management?
cards.back: Source segregation means separating different types of waste at the point of generation — i.e. at home, school, or office — BEFORE it is mixed. Typically: green/wet bin for biodegradable waste (food scraps, vegetable peels) and blue/white bin for dry/non-biodegradable waste (plastic, paper, metal, glass). Importance: once waste is mixed, it is very difficult and expensive to separate. Mixed waste often ends up entirely in landfills. Segregated biodegradable waste can go directly to composting; segregated dry waste to recyclers — diverting large volumes from landfills. BBMP Bengaluru mandates two-bin source segregation in all households.
cards.memory_hook: Segregate at source = sort BEFORE mixing, not after. Mixed garbage = one big problem. Sorted garbage = many useful resources. Once you mix curry and plastic in one bin, both go to landfill. Keep them separate from the START.

cards.front: How does recycling paper help the environment? State two specific facts.
cards.back: Recycling paper provides major environmental benefits: (1) Saves trees: 1 tonne of recycled paper saves 17 trees. Trees are cut for wood pulp to make virgin paper — recycling reduces this demand. (2) Saves water: 1 tonne of recycled paper saves approximately 26,000 litres of water (paper manufacturing is extremely water-intensive). (3) Saves energy: recycled paper production uses 60–70% less energy than virgin paper production. (4) Reduces landfill: paper is a large fraction of municipal waste; recycling diverts it from landfills. (5) Reduces CO₂: less energy use = less fossil fuel burning = less CO₂.
cards.memory_hook: Paper recycling math: 1 tonne recycled = 17 trees + 26,000 litres water + energy saved. Every time you give old newspapers to the kabadiwala, you're saving trees. 17 trees per tonne — that's a small forest per paper factory per day.

cards.front: How long does plastic take to decompose? Why is this a serious problem?
cards.back: Most common plastics (polyethylene bags, PET bottles, polystyrene) take 100–1000+ years to decompose in the environment. During this time, they: (1) Break into smaller pieces called microplastics — which enter the food chain through water and soil. (2) Entangle and kill marine animals and birds. (3) Block drains, causing urban flooding. (4) Release toxic chemicals as they slowly degrade. (5) Accumulate in landfills indefinitely. India generates 9.4 million tonnes of plastic waste annually — less than 30% is recycled. The rest goes to landfills, water bodies, or is burned. Karnataka banned single-use plastics under 40 microns in 2016 to combat this.
cards.memory_hook: A plastic bag used for 20 minutes lives for 500 years. Think about that ratio: 20 minutes of use, 500 years of pollution. That plastic bag you got at the supermarket will outlive everyone reading this textbook.

cards.front: Bengaluru's BBMP uses two-bin collection. What goes in each bin?
cards.back: BBMP's two-bin system: Green bin (wet waste / biodegradable): vegetable and fruit peels, cooked food waste, flowers, leaves, garden waste, egg shells, tea bags. This waste goes to composting plants or biogas plants. White/Blue bin (dry waste / non-biodegradable): plastic wrappers and bottles, glass bottles and jars, paper and cardboard, metal cans, cloth. This waste is sent to dry waste collection centres (DWCCs) where it is further sorted and sent to recyclers. Hazardous waste (batteries, medicines, chemicals, e-waste) is collected separately through special drives. Key rule: keep the two streams completely separate — mixed waste is very difficult to recycle.
cards.memory_hook: Green = Gone-to-compost. White = Will-be-recycled. Two bins, two destinations, two lives for two types of waste. Remember it as: Green for the garden (compost), White for the factory (recycling).

cards.front: How do earthworms help in vermicomposting? What is vermicompost used for?
cards.back: Earthworms consume organic waste and digest it through their gut. Their castings (excretions/worm poop) — called vermicompost — are rich in nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and beneficial microorganisms. The earthworm gut dramatically accelerates decomposition — what takes 4–8 weeks by microbial composting takes only 2–4 weeks with earthworms. Uses of vermicompost: soil amendment for farms and gardens (improves soil fertility and structure), potted plant nutrition, organic farming (replaces chemical fertilisers), and export (vermicompost is sold as premium organic fertiliser). Earthworms also aerate the soil by burrowing, further improving soil health.
cards.memory_hook: Earthworms = nature's composting machines + soil engineers. They eat garbage and produce gold (vermicompost). They tunnel through soil and aerate it. A healthy farm soil has millions of earthworms — they're the underground workforce you never see.

cards.front: Why is e-waste (electronic waste) a special concern?
cards.back: E-waste (discarded electronic devices: old phones, computers, TVs, batteries, cables) is one of the fastest-growing waste categories. Problems: (1) Non-biodegradable — lasts centuries in landfills. (2) Contains toxic materials — lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium, PCBs — which leach into soil and groundwater. (3) Valuable resources — gold, silver, copper, palladium inside old phones and computers are wasted when e-waste goes to landfill. (4) Informal recycling — untrained workers in informal sectors who dismantle e-waste are exposed to toxic fumes and chemicals. India's E-Waste Management Rules 2016 require manufacturers to take back and safely recycle their products. Bengaluru as India's 'Silicon Valley' generates large volumes of e-waste.
cards.memory_hook: E-waste = toxic + valuable at the same time. Your old phone has gold inside and lead beside it. Throwing it in landfill wastes the gold and poisons the water. The solution: authorised e-waste recyclers who safely separate the valuable from the toxic.

cards.front: How did Bengaluru's 2012 garbage crisis happen, and what change did it force?
cards.back: In 2012, Bengaluru's landfills — especially at Mandur — became so overloaded that they were releasing toxic leachate into nearby streams and groundwater. Villagers near Mandur blockaded garbage trucks, refusing to allow more waste to be dumped. Bengaluru's garbage had nowhere to go — waste piled up on streets for days. Public outrage and court orders forced BBMP to act. Changes brought: (1) Mandatory source segregation (two-bin system) was introduced city-wide. (2) Decentralised composting units were set up in apartments and housing societies. (3) Dry Waste Collection Centres (DWCCs) were established to handle recyclables. (4) Karnataka Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 formalized these requirements statewide. Lesson: garbage mismanagement affects everyone.
cards.memory_hook: Bengaluru 2012 = when the city choked on its own waste. Villagers said NO. Bengaluru had no choice but to change. Sometimes environmental solutions come from communities standing up, not just from government policy.

cards.front: How does Mysuru serve as a model for waste management in Karnataka?
cards.back: Mysuru has consistently ranked among India's cleanest cities in the Swachh Survekshan (Clean India Survey) annual rankings. Key practices: (1) High source segregation compliance — most households actively separate wet and dry waste. (2) Large-scale composting of wet waste — reduces landfill dependency. (3) Active door-to-door collection with segregated vehicles. (4) Community awareness campaigns and active RWA participation. (5) Reduced use of single-use plastic in markets — many vendors use cloth and paper bags. (6) Functional Dry Waste Collection Centres. Mysuru proves that with community participation and systematic planning, a medium-sized Indian city can manage its waste effectively and sustainably.
cards.memory_hook: Mysuru = Karnataka's cleanliness champion. The same city famous for Mysore Pak (sweet) is now famous for waste management. Clean city = clean habits × consistent systems × community participation.

cards.front: A student produces the following waste in one school day: orange peel, a plastic straw, rough paper with notes, a pen that ran out of ink (plastic body), and a cloth kerchief. Classify and suggest what to do with each.
cards.back: Orange peel — biodegradable → put in green/wet bin or school compost pit. Plastic straw — non-biodegradable → dry bin → but better: REFUSE straws in the first place (Reduce). Rough paper with notes — biodegradable → use the blank side first (Reuse), then give to paper recycler or use as rough paper (Recycle). Empty plastic pen — non-biodegradable → collect for e-waste/plastic recycling; better: buy a refillable pen next time (Reduce). Cloth kerchief — biodegradable + reusable → wash and reuse; if torn, use as cleaning cloth (Reuse/Reduce; avoids tissue paper waste). This analysis shows the 3Rs applied to real school life.
cards.memory_hook: Every item has a 3R story. Ask: Can I REDUCE by not buying/using this? Can I REUSE it again? Can I RECYCLE it? Only if all three fail → dispose responsibly. Apply this to every item you discard.
